title: Writing a PEEL paragraph
examples: When I write an essay, how do I make sure my points connect well?
Can you show me an example of a PEEL paragraph about a book?
Is PEEL only for writing arguments, or can I use it elsewhere?

explain.say: Today we are learning a useful writing structure called PEEL.

draw.text: P: Point, E: Evidence, E: Explain, L: Link

explain.say: The first part is the Point, where you state your main idea for the paragraph.

items: Start with a clear topic sentence.
This tells the reader what you will discuss.

explain.say: Next, you need Evidence, which is a specific fact or example to back up your point.
Then, you must Explain, which means you tell the reader how the evidence proves your point.

draw.text: Explain: How does it prove it?

explain.say: Finally, you Link the paragraph back to the main topic or the next idea.

draw.text: Link: Connect to the next idea.

explain.say: For a real-life example, imagine you are writing about recycling.

faq.q: What does PEEL stand for again?
faq.a: PEEL stands for Point, Evidence, Explain, and Link. This structure helps make your writing very clear.
asks: What does the acronym PEEL mean in writing?
Can you remind me of the steps in PEEL?

faq.q: Do I need a different sentence for each part?
faq.a: Yes, try to start each part with a clear sentence. This helps the reader follow your argument easily.
asks: Should I use transition words between the parts?
Is it okay if my sentences are very short?

faq.a: Good evidence is something specific, like a direct quote or a piece of data. It must come from your source material.
asks: Can I just say something I think is true?
Is a general idea enough for evidence?

faq.q: How long should my explanation be?
faq.a: Your explanation should be the longest part. You need enough sentences to fully convince the reader of your point.
asks: Do I need a whole paragraph for explaining?
Should I explain everything I know about the topic?

faq.q: What is the link sentence for?
faq.a: The link sentence smoothly guides the reader to the next paragraph's topic. It shows how your ideas connect.
asks: Why do I need a link at the end?
Does the link have to be about the same topic?

facts: A Point states the main argument of the paragraph.
Evidence must be specific information from a source.
The Explain section analyzes how the evidence supports the point.
The Link sentence connects the paragraph to the next idea.

quiz.say: A student writes: 'The character was brave. For example, he faced the dragon alone. This shows he had great courage. This idea connects to his actions later.' Which part is the student doing when they say, 'This shows he had great courage'?
quiz.why: This sentence tells the reader how the evidence proves the point, which is the job of explaining.

wrong.0: The point is the main sentence, not the analysis of the evidence.
wrong.1: Evidence is the fact itself, like 'he faced the dragon alone'.
wrong.2: The link looks forward, connecting to the next idea, not analyzing the current one.

quiz.say: Which step comes immediately after providing a specific piece of evidence?
quiz.why: After you give the evidence, you must explain what that evidence means for your point.

wrong.0: The point always comes first, setting up the whole paragraph.
wrong.1: The link comes at the very end, summarizing and moving on.
wrong.2: You cannot give evidence twice in a row; you must explain it first.

quiz.say: A writer ends a paragraph with: 'Therefore, this shows how important teamwork is for the whole team.' This sentence is best described as the:
quiz.show: Link: Connecting to the next idea.
quiz.why: This sentence wraps up the argument and prepares the reader for the topic coming next.

wrong.0: Explaining analyzes the evidence; linking moves the reader forward.
wrong.2: The point is the start of the paragraph, not the end.
wrong.3: Evidence needs to be a specific fact, not a summary statement.
